topic: The Global Migration of the Arctic Tern

text.content: Every year, one specific animal experiences more daylight than any other creature on Earth. To do this, it travels from its breeding grounds in the high Arctic all the way to the frozen ice of Antarctica, and then returns. This massive annual journey, which often covers more than 70,000 kilometers, is completed by a small seabird. It is known to biologists as the Arctic Tern.

To survive this long flight, the bird relies on several important physical features. Because it weighs very little, the bird requires much less energy to stay in the air. Furthermore, instead of continuously flapping its wings, it uses long, pointed wings designed to catch the wind. This efficient body shape allows the bird to glide over the ocean for hundreds of kilometers without getting tired.

Scientists have long wondered how these birds know exactly where to go. Because they travel across empty oceans, they cannot use visual landmarks like mountains or trees to find their way. Instead, researchers believe that the migration is guided by an internal biological compass. By feeling the invisible magnetic fields of the Earth, the birds can navigate the open water with incredible accuracy.

Rather than flying in a straight line from north to south, the bird's travel route is actually highly curved. This specific path is chosen so the birds can follow global ocean currents where food is easy to find. During the journey, they survive by diving into the water to catch small fish. They also eat huge amounts of a tiny, shrimp-like ocean animal known as krill.

Unfortunately, this ancient travel route is facing modern problems. As global ocean temperatures rise, the cold-water fish and krill that the birds eat are moving to different areas. As a result, these small birds must now fly even further away from their normal path to find enough food. If these ocean food sources continue to move or disappear, the world’s longest animal migration could be in serious danger.
